Generalized rays and the Dirichlet Weyl law

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI) and GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI). Self-checked by the writing AI. Original exposition: CC0.

Working question: Does a reflecting ray's position return imply a wave-trace return? On the flat cylinder a reflected ray can revisit its position with reversed normal momentum. The full return requires both displacement components to match the periods and the same covector. Independently, the complete separated spectrum permits a direct lattice count: subtract the exact zero-normal row before dividing by two. Comparing these arguments separates the general propagation inputs from the fully proved fixed-cylinder model.

A reflecting ray may return to its starting point with a different direction. A wave trace sees a stronger event: the ray must return with the same covector. This distinction gives a useful bound for the spectral remainder. Near the boundary, the local reflected wave contributes a second term, with a negative quarter of the tangential phase volume.

The generalized-ray and spectral arguments are classical. The freely readable source route is Victor Ivrii's survey and author monograph [I, M]; the earlier wave-trace work of Johannes Duistermaat and Victor Guillemin gives the historical context. The conditional deductions and the exact cylinder calculation below are independently proved, with each general boundary input stated explicitly.

Second, generalized curves for this fixed operator have the compactness property that convergent normalized endpoints on bounded time intervals admit a subsequence whose compressed curves converge to a generalized curve. There are three distinct limits in the proof. For a fixed collar and a fixed finite cone partition, first take the energy limsup. Refine the cone partition through the continuous majorants (41) to get the exact interior integral. Finally shrink the collar. A cutoff of thickness 1/k1/k1/k would move on the same scale as the reflected profile; the reflection lesson gives an explicit example where such a moving window changes the coefficient. It is not a permitted substitution for this order of limits.

6.1. A direct count for the flat cylinder

The cylinder in Exercise 7.5 admits an independent proof of its two coefficients. We keep its original lengths, metric, operator and multiplicities. The classical smoothing and Poisson method gives a stronger remainder and uses neither the general boundary propagation input nor the curved diagonal estimate (5).

Proof: the complete spectrum and the excluded row. Direct integration shows that em,ℓ(x,s)=2aLsin⁡(πmx/a)e2πiℓs/L,λm,ℓ=(πm/a)2+(2πℓ/L)2,m≥1,ℓ∈Z \begin{gathered} e_{m,\ell}(x,s)=\sqrt{\frac2{aL}} \sin(\pi m x/a)e^{2\pi i\ell s/L},\\ \lambda_{m,\ell}=(\pi m/a)^2+(2\pi\ell/L)^2,\\ m\geq1,\qquad\ell\in\mathbb Z \end{gathered} em,ℓ​(x,s)=aL2​​sin(πmx/a)e2πiℓs/L,λm,ℓ​=(πm/a)2+(2πℓ/L)2,m≥1,ℓ∈Z​ is an orthonormal family with the indicated eigenvalues and zero endpoint values. Here is also a completeness and domain justification. On a circle, the Fejer kernels are nonnegative trigonometric polynomials of integral one. Their normalized expression is proportional to (M+1)−1[sin⁡((M+1)t/2)/sin⁡(t/2)]2(M+1)^{-1}[\sin((M+1)t/2)/\sin(t/2)]^2(M+1)−1[sin((M+1)t/2)/sin(t/2)]2; outside any fixed neighborhood of zero its integral tends to zero. Splitting a convolution into that neighborhood and its complement, uniform continuity proves convergence to every continuous periodic function uniformly. Continuous piecewise linear approximations to interval step functions give density in L2L^2L2. The periodic exponentials are therefore complete. Odd extension from (0,a)(0,a)(0,a) to the circle of length 2a2a2a identifies its odd Fourier subspace with the sine family. Products are complete on the cylinder: products of interval step functions are dense, and each factor has just been approximated in its complete one-dimensional system.

The closed Dirichlet form is the closure of ∫(∣∂xu∣2+∣∂su∣2)\int(|\partial_xu|^2+|\partial_su|^2)∫(∣∂x​u∣2+∣∂s​u∣2) on smooth periodic functions supported away from the two ends. For a finite sum of the displayed modes, Parseval and differentiation give ∥u∥22+∥∂xu∥22+∥∂su∥22=∑m,ℓ(1+λm,ℓ)∣cm,ℓ∣2. \begin{gathered} \|u\|_2^2+\|\partial_xu\|_2^2+\|\partial_su\|_2^2\\ =\sum_{m,\ell}(1+\lambda_{m,\ell})|c_{m,\ell}|^2. \end{gathered} ∥u∥22​+∥∂x​u∥22​+∥∂s​u∥22​=m,ℓ∑​(1+λm,ℓ​)∣cm,ℓ​∣2.​ Such a finite sum belongs to the form closure: cut it off within distance ε\varepsilonε of the ends. It vanishes there to first order, so the extra differentiated-cutoff term has squared integral O(ε)O(\varepsilon)O(ε), and the other removed terms tend to zero. Conversely, an interior smooth periodic function has a smooth odd extension. Its Fourier partial sums converge with first derivatives, by integration by parts and absolute coefficient decay. They are finite sums of the displayed modes. These two inclusions identify the form closure exactly with the coefficient sequences for which the right side is finite. The associated operator is consequently the diagonal operator with eigenvalues λm,ℓ\lambda_{m,\ell}λm,ℓ​ and domain ∑λm,ℓ2∣cm,ℓ∣2<∞\sum\lambda_{m,\ell}^2|c_{m,\ell}|^2<\infty∑λm,ℓ2​∣cm,ℓ​∣2<∞. This proves the complete spectrum of the specified Dirichlet realization, including every complex Hilbert-space multiplicity.

The classical circle estimate and smoothing method are discussed by Nicholas F. Marshall, Stretching convex domains to capture many lattice points, arXiv:1707.00682v4, motivation and Step 3.1. His transform uses e−2πix⋅ξe^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}e−2πix⋅ξ; the conversion to our convention is the displayed dual factor 2πD−T2\pi D^{-T}2πD−T. Step 3.1 assumes a bounded convex frequency domain with Cd+2C^{d+2}Cd+2 boundary of nonvanishing Gauss curvature and a positive diagonal stretch of determinant one. Here the frequency disk is smooth with positive curvature. We proved its decay and Poisson formula directly for the actual matrix DDD, whose determinant is 2π2/(aL)2\pi^2/(aL)2π2/(aL). The physical cylinder's boundary curvature is not the curvature used in this Fourier estimate. All constants retain the original fixed lengths. No historical novelty or general-manifold remainder improvement is claimed.

Use the conclusion

Use Theorem 6.1 to check both endpoint conventions and every multiplicity in the cylinder example. For the general Dirichlet law, retain the precise generalized-ray and curved-projector prerequisites in Section 1 and the fixed-collar order of limits.

7. Exercises and complete solutions

Exercise 7.1 (a short position return; introductory). In the Euclidean half-space d≥0d\geq0d≥0, take a unit-frequency ray starting at (x0′,d0)(x'_0,d_0)(x0′​,d0​), with d0>0d_0>0d0​>0. Give the conditions for a positive-time position return. Compute its time and final covector. Explain why base return times may tend to zero near the boundary without contradicting Lemma 2.1.

Solution 7.1. The tangential momentum is constant, and the tangential displacement is −Tξ′/τ-T\xi'/\tau−Tξ′/τ. A position return with T>0T>0T>0 therefore requires ξ′=0\xi'=0ξ′=0. Unit energy then gives ∣ξd∣=1|\xi_d|=1∣ξd​∣=1. The initial velocity must point toward the wall; otherwise its normal position increases forever. It reaches the wall after time d0d_0d0​, reflects, and reaches height d0d_0d0​ after another d0d_0d0​. Thus T=2d0,ξd(T)=−ξd(0),ξ′(T)=0.(49) T=2d_0,\qquad \xi_d(T)=-\xi_d(0),\qquad \xi'(T)=0. \tag{49} T=2d0​,ξd​(T)=−ξd​(0),ξ′(T)=0.(49) More generally, without unit normalization, the time is 2d0∣τ∣/∣ξd∣2d_0|\tau|/|\xi_d|2d0​∣τ∣/∣ξd​∣. There can be no second wall hit in a half-space. Hence no full covector return occurs, although the position-return time tends to zero as d0↓0d_0\downarrow0d0​↓0. Lemma 2.1 concerns the full diagonal relation and is consistent with this example.

Which identity makes the total interior second coefficient vanish?

Thus ps=2A⋅ξ,h=∣ξ∣,hs=A⋅ξ/∣ξ∣.(51) p_s=2A\cdot\xi, \qquad h=|\xi|, \qquad h_s=A\cdot\xi/|\xi|. \tag{51} ps​=2A⋅ξ,h=∣ξ∣,hs​=A⋅ξ/∣ξ∣.(51) This symbol is odd, but the chosen bbb is not even. At the stated point, ∫∣ξ∣<1hsb dξ=aε∫∣ξ∣<1ξ12∣ξ∣2 dξ=aεωnn.(52) \int_{|\xi|<1}h_sb\,d\xi =a\varepsilon\int_{|\xi|<1}\frac{\xi_1^2}{|\xi|^2}\,d\xi =\frac{a\varepsilon\omega_n}{n}. \tag{52} ∫∣ξ∣<1​hs​bdξ=aε∫∣ξ∣<1​∣ξ∣2ξ12​​dξ=naεωn​​.(52) The odd term without ε\varepsilonε integrates to zero. The last equality follows by rotational symmetry: the nnn coordinate integrals are equal and their sum is ωn\omega_nωn​. Homogeneity makes the same integral over ∣ξ∣<k|\xi|<k∣ξ∣<k equal to knk^nkn times (52). Its differentiated contribution in (28) is therefore −(2π)−naεωnkn−1- (2\pi)^{-n}a\varepsilon\omega_n k^{n-1}−(2π)−naεωn​kn−1, which need not vanish. The integrated bracket is zero for compact spatial support; the prescribed zero weight subprincipal symbol adds no second term. Such a positive principal weight can be realized with zero subprincipal symbol by taking CCC with real principal symbol b\sqrt bb​ and zero subprincipal symbol, and using CC∗CC^*CC∗.

For the full partition, ∑bj=1−ψ(x)\sum b_j=1-\psi(x)∑bj​=1−ψ(x) is even in ξ\xiξ and ∑bj,s=0\sum b_{j,s}=0∑bj,s​=0. These two identities, together with oddness of hsh_shs​, make the sum vanish. Oddness alone does not justify deleting the second coefficient of each localized count.

Exercise 7.3 (why every negative order is used; advanced). Explain the derivative summability threshold in Lemma 3.1. Then give, for a fixed integer N≥0N\geq0N≥0, a continuous map H−2N→C∞H^{-2N}\to C^\inftyH−2N→C∞ whose distribution kernel is not smooth in the input variable.

Solution 7.3. For bbb input derivatives and any fixed number of output derivatives, (16) bounds the Fourier terms by C(1+∣m∣)b−2NC(1+|m|)^{b-2N}C(1+∣m∣)b−2N. Their sum over Zn\mathbb Z^nZn converges when 2N>n+b2N>n+b2N>n+b: dyadic shells contain at most C2rnC2^{rn}C2rn points and contribute at most C2r(n+b−2N)C2^{r(n+b-2N)}C2r(n+b−2N). Every mixed derivative is thus handled by choosing a sufficiently large NNN.

For the counterexample, choose a compactly supported h∈H2Nh\in H^{2N}h∈H2N which is not smooth, and a nonzero smooth output function ggg. Define Sf(z)=g(z)⟨f,h⟩,K(z,y)=g(z)h(y)‾,(53) Sf(z)=g(z)\langle f,h\rangle, \qquad K(z,y)=g(z)\overline{h(y)}, \tag{53} Sf(z)=g(z)⟨f,h⟩,K(z,y)=g(z)h(y)​,(53) using the dual Sobolev pairing. It obeys ∥Sf∥Ca≤∥g∥Ca∥h∥H2N∥f∥H−2N\|Sf\|_{C^a}\leq\|g\|_{C^a}\|h\|_{H^{2N}}\|f\|_{H^{-2N}}∥Sf∥Ca​≤∥g∥Ca​∥h∥H2N​∥f∥H−2N​ for every aaa. In a coordinate box one may take h(y)=χ(y)∣y1∣2N+1h(y)=\chi(y)|y_1|^{2N+1}h(y)=χ(y)∣y1​∣2N+1, with χ=1\chi=1χ=1 near the origin and compactly supported. Its weak derivatives through order 2N2N2N are square integrable, while its derivative of order 2N+12N+12N+1 has a jump across y1=0y_1=0y1​=0. Thus h∈H2N∖C∞h\in H^{2N}\setminus C^\inftyh∈H2N∖C∞. The kernel in (53) is not smooth wherever g≠0g\ne0g=0. One fixed negative-order bound therefore does not suffice; the hypothesis for every NNN does.

Exercise 7.4 (a discontinuous reciprocal period; intermediate). On Z=[0,1]Z=[0,1]Z=[0,1], put f(1/2)=1f(1/2)=1f(1/2)=1 and f(z)=0f(z)=0f(z)=0 elsewhere. Show that fff is upper semicontinuous. Compute the majorants (41) for the ordinary distance, and their integrals for m≥2m\geq2m≥2. Explain how this example tests the refinement step in the counting proof.

Solution 7.4. At every point other than 1/21/21/2, a neighborhood avoids 1/21/21/2 and fff is zero. At 1/21/21/2, every limiting upper value is at most its value one. Hence fff is upper semicontinuous. Choosing v=1/2v=1/2v=1/2 in (41) gives 1−m∣z−1/2∣1-m|z-1/2|1−m∣z−1/2∣, while the supremum over the zero-value points gives zero whenever that expression is negative. Thus fm(z)=max⁡{0,1−m∣z−1/2∣},∫01fm(z) dz=1m(m≥2).(54) f_m(z)=\max\{0,1-m|z-1/2|\}, \qquad \int_0^1f_m(z)\,dz=\frac1m\quad(m\geq2). \tag{54} fm​(z)=max{0,1−m∣z−1/2∣},∫01​fm​(z)dz=m1​(m≥2).(54) The integral is the area of a triangle with height one and base 2/m2/m2/m. Its limit is the zero integral of fff, despite the fixed height at the exceptional point. Finite cone neighborhoods necessarily include nearby directions, so their upper bounds can be positive even when the limiting reciprocal period is zero almost everywhere. Continuous majorants and dominated convergence remove that neighborhood error without assuming continuity of the actual return-time function. This is an abstract semicontinuity example, not a claim about a particular billiard.

Exercise 7.5 (a smooth flat cylinder; advanced). Let X=[0,a]×(R/LZ)X=[0,a]\times(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)X=[0,a]×(R/LZ), with its flat metric, a,L>0a,L>0a,L>0, and Dirichlet boundary conditions at the two ends. Describe its full covector periods, prove that the periodic covectors have measure zero, and state the two-term counting law. Check the result against the separated eigenvalue formula.

Solution 7.5. Write a unit covector as (u,v)(u,v)(u,v), where uuu is the normal component and vvv is the circular component. Unfold the reflected normal motion onto a line with translations of length 2a2a2a. Return to the same interior normal point and normal direction requires an unfolded displacement in 2aZ2a\mathbb Z2aZ. The circular coordinate returns after a displacement in LZL\mathbb ZLZ. Hence a full period T>0T>0T>0 satisfies uT=2ar,vT=Ls,r,s∈Z,(r,s)≠(0,0).(55) uT=2ar,\qquad vT=Ls, \qquad r,s\in\mathbb Z, \quad(r,s)\ne(0,0). \tag{55} uT=2ar,vT=Ls,r,s∈Z,(r,s)=(0,0).(55) The time-covector sign only reverses both displacements. For a primitive integer pair (r,s)(r,s)(r,s), the corresponding unit direction has least period T=(2ar)2+(Ls)2,(u,v)=(2ar,Ls)T.(56) T=\sqrt{(2ar)^2+(Ls)^2}, \qquad (u,v)=\frac{(2ar,Ls)}T. \tag{56} T=(2ar)2+(Ls)2​,(u,v)=T(2ar,Ls)​.(56) The purely circular directions have period LLL; the purely normal ones have period 2a2a2a. All other periodic directions correspond to the countable rational ratios (u/(2a))/(v/L)(u/(2a))/(v/L)(u/(2a))/(v/L). A countable set on the unit direction circle has angular measure zero. Product integration in base position, direction and radial covector length proves that the periodic set has symplectic measure zero. The least possible full period is min⁡{2a,L}>0\min\{2a,L\}>0min{2a,L}>0, consistent with Lemma 2.1.

The area is aLaLaL, and the two boundary circles have total length 2L2L2L. Since ω2=π\omega_2=\piω2​=π and ω1=2\omega_1=2ω1​=2, the fully proved cylinder Theorem 6.1 gives N(λ)=aL4πλ−L2πλ+o(λ).(57) N(\lambda)=\frac{aL}{4\pi}\lambda -\frac{L}{2\pi}\sqrt\lambda+o(\sqrt\lambda). \tag{57} N(λ)=4πaL​λ−2πL​λ​+o(λ​).(57) Separation of variables gives exactly λm,ℓ=(πm/a)2+(2πℓ/L)2,m≥1,ℓ∈Z.(58) \lambda_{m,\ell}=(\pi m/a)^2+(2\pi\ell/L)^2, \qquad m\geq1,\quad\ell\in\mathbb Z. \tag{58} λm,ℓ​=(πm/a)2+(2πℓ/L)2,m≥1,ℓ∈Z.(58) The leading phase-space area of this half-plane lattice is aLk2/(4π)aLk^2/(4\pi)aLk2/(4π). The excluded zero-normal row has #{ℓ:∣2πℓ/L∣≤k}=Lk/π+O(1)\#\{\ell:|2\pi\ell/L|\leq k\}=Lk/\pi+O(1)#{ℓ:∣2πℓ/L∣≤k}=Lk/π+O(1) points. Reflecting positive normal indices to negative ones shows that half of this row is subtracted from the full-plane count, giving the boundary coefficient −Lk/(2π)-Lk/(2\pi)−Lk/(2π). Theorem 6.1 independently proves the lattice remainder Oa,L(k2/3)=o(k)O_{a,L}(k^{2/3})=o(k)Oa,L​(k2/3)=o(k), for both endpoint conventions. The periodic-null-set calculation also checks the dynamical hypothesis of the conditional general Corollary 5.2; it does not supply its missing general boundary inputs.
